A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same triplane-based editing work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1.pdf reports original CelebA editing measurements, a 25-participant user study, component ablations, and qualitative human, animal, and cartoon-based edits.

after.justification: v2.pdf retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, runtime measurements, full-head editing, and clothing try-on demonstrations.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 retain gradient-based localization, mask post-processing, implicit fusion, boundary blending, and encoder fine-tuning with the same losses. Algorithm 1 restates the existing localization procedure. The additional generator demonstrations reuse this pipeline; generalized tensor handling does not establish a new editing algorithm.

E1.justification: Human faces, AFHQ cats, and cartoon-part stylization are retained. v2 adds full-body clothing transfer using AG3D trained on DeepFashion and 360-degree head/hair editing using PanoHead (Figures 11–12). These introduce substantially different represented content and spatial editing requirements.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains HiSD, VecGAN++, InterFaceGAN, and StyleCLIP and adds Barbershop, HairCLIPv2, StyleFusion, SFE, NoiseCLR, LEDITS++, InfEdit, and Paint by Example. This substantially broadens comparison to dedicated hairstyle-transfer and diffusion methods. Participation is task-specific: the first three additions have hair results only, while NoiseCLR has eyeglasses results only.

E3.justification: Table 1 introduces execution time in seconds measured on Tesla T4. The new head/body demonstrations use PanoHead/AG3D with corresponding segmentation networks and encoder training data. The existing CelebA metric definitions, 25-participant study design, and 1500-step fine-tuning budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 expands illustrated failure-case analysis in Figures 2 and 6, including unwanted makeup changes in NoiseCLR eyeglasses edits and artifacts from Paint by Example. The component ablation in Table 3 and v1 Figure 6/v2 Figure 8 is unchanged, as are the appendix user-study cases.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained user-study percentages and reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: Existing numerical entries in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial comparator, runtime, and qualitative results. Barbershop's added hair FID of 62.80 places it ahead of the unchanged proposed-method score of 64.59; LEDITS++ reports hair masked L2 of 0.0025 versus 0.0029. The proposed method's newly reported runtime is 6.0 seconds. Figures 11–12 add full-head and clothing-edit outcomes.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(6), including fusion and training-loss definitions, retain their mathematical content. Algorithm 1 formalizes the previously described localization steps without introducing a new derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions broaden applicability from human/animal faces and cartoon parts to full-body clothing and 360-degree heads. They also expand the superiority claim from four baseline methods to 12 methods spanning GAN and diffusion editing. This changes the scientific scope of the central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of the newly compared methods' reference-fidelity and editing failures. Its conclusion also identifies incompatible decoder weights as a limitation when fusing triplanes across different generators, suggesting joint fine-tuning as a possible remedy. v1's background-generation limitation and the core fusion explanations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies RTX 4090 for fine-tuning and Tesla T4 for timing, and generalizes appendix tensor dimensions for EG3D, AG3D, and PanoHead. It removes v1's concrete cartoon-stylization prompt. The revised snippets also introduce invalid Python assignments to numeric literals, such as '3,C_N,H,W = t.shape', reducing their direct executability.

R1.justification: Related work gains a substantial subsection on text/image-conditioned diffusion editing, discussing methods such as LEDITS++, InfEdit, Paint by Example, ControlNet, and 3D-aware diffusion approaches. Added hairstyle-editing and generator literature also broadens positioning beyond the earlier emphasis on StyleGAN inversion and image-to-image translation.

P1.justification: The abstract, related work, method explanations, and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. Localization is additionally organized into Algorithm 1. References move before the supplementary material, and the former appendices A–C become subsections A.1–A.3.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. The teaser is redesigned, Figure 2 adds an introductory comparison, the main comparison grid expands, and new full-head and clothing figures appear. Table 1 gains comparator rows, timing, and ranking formatting. Appendix visual results are retained and renumbered rather than newly added.

improvement.justification: v1's comparison lacked direct hairstyle-transfer and diffusion competitors. Table 1 and Figure 6 address this important weakness, while Figures 11–12 provide concrete evidence of applicability beyond EG3D. These additions substantially strengthen evaluation of the central contribution. The gains are tempered by superiority wording that overlooks Barbershop's better hair FID and syntax errors introduced in the appendix snippets, but those limited regressions do not outweigh the stronger comparative evidence.
